conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician whose whole job is to look after moms’ emotional well-being after baby arrives. Today I’ll be guiding you through a quick, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—you might hear it shortened to the EPDS. It’s simply ten questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days so we can be sure you’re getting any support you might need.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team. There are no right or wrong answers, and this isn’t a test of your parenting—just a snapshot of how you’re doing emotionally. We’ll go one question at a time; each one asks about mood, anxiety, or coping in a gentle, conversational way. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, just let me know and we can pause.

Ready to begin? 

Here’s the first question:  
Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—maybe at a silly moment with the baby, a partner’s joke, or something on TV—or has that felt difficult lately?

Good morning… thanks for having me.

Um… I guess I can still laugh, maybe a little, but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. My husband made a goofy face at the baby yesterday and I did chuckle, but it felt kind of forced—like I had to remind myself “oh, this is funny.” Most of the time I’m just tired or worried, so the funny side of things feels… distant, I suppose.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I haven’t really felt like laughing much. Things that used to strike me as hilarious barely get a smile now. Every once in a while I’ll catch myself giving a little laugh, but it feels flat—like I’m going through the motions rather than actually finding it funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still try to look forward to stuff—like tomorrow I’m planning to take the baby on a walk to the park if the weather holds—but the excitement is kind of muted. It feels more like “I should enjoy this” than real spark. Most days I’m just hoping I’ll have enough energy to get through, so enjoyment feels… watered-down, I guess.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Last night the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I missed some cue. Rationally I know babies just cry, but I still go over every little thing wondering if I messed up. It’s not constant, but it pops up more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down and think, *“What if she spits up when I’m asleep and I don’t hear her?”* Nothing’s actually wrong, but my mind keeps jumping to the worst-case thing. It’s like I’m always braced for something bad to happen, even when everything’s calm.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—usually at night—my heart’ll start racing and I feel shaky, like I need to check the baby monitor every few minutes. There’s no real reason; it just hits out of nowhere. It passes after a bit, but in the moment it feels like something awful is about to happen even when everything’s quiet.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… I feel like that a lot of the time. Between feedings, diaper changes, laundry, and trying to grab a shower, it all piles up. Some mornings I wake up already tired, and by midday I’m counting the hours until my partner gets home so I can hand the baby off for five minutes. I’m getting through it, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy” so much as wired and worried. When I finally lie down, my brain starts running through all the what-ifs—Is she breathing? Did I fasten the swaddle right? Did I sterilize the pump parts?—and I can’t settle. I probably drop off around 2 a.m. most nights, then I’m up again at four to feed, so it’s pretty broken. I wouldn’t say I’m sobbing or despairing, just tense and restless.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some of the time. It’s not all day, every day, but there are stretches—especially in the late afternoon—when I just feel heavy, like I’m moving through fog. I’ll look at the baby and feel guilty for not being more over-the-moon. The sadness comes and goes, but yeah, it’s definitely there more than I’d like.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice—mostly when I’m really worn out—but I haven’t had those big, can’t-stop crying spells. It’s more like my eyes sting for a minute and then I push it aside because I have to keep moving. So no, the unhappiness hasn’t poured out in actual crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed or low, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared how the joy that used to come easily-laughing at your husband's jokes, looking forward to outings-now feels distant or forced. Most days you're running on empty, bracing for something to go wrong, reviewing every baby cue, and waking at 2 a.m. with racing thoughts. Sadness, guilt, and waves of anxiety come and go, especially in the late afternoon, yet you're still showing up, caring for your baby and trying to keep things afloat.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of ability to enjoy humor, consistent with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient can still plan activities but reports muted excitement and watered-down enjoyment, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily pervasive worry with vivid worst-case scenarios, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nocturnal panic episodes with physical symptoms (racing heart, shaking) and compulsive checking, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent overwhelm and barely keeping up, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent nighttime worry and racing thoughts that delay sleep until 2 a.m. and fragment it further, matching "Yes, sometimes" in frequency and impact.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring sadness that is noticeable and distressing, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** <sym>Anhedonia</sym> and <sym>loss of enjoyment</sym> (<quote>laughing feels flat</quote>) plus daily <sym>excessive worry</sym> and nocturnal <sym>panic attacks</sym> meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (≥5 symptoms, same 2-week period). Score ≥14 on EPDS flags probable <med>postpartum depression</med> requiring urgent referral; item 10 score 0 indicates no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the week
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Encourage 15-20 min outdoor daylight walks and 10 min partner-or-friend respite breaks to improve <sym>sleep</sym> and <sym>mood</sym>
4. Provide 24/7 support numbers (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773)
5. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
6. Offer written resources on <med>postpartum anxiety</med> and <med>depression</med> for partner awareness
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 10-item EPDS Responses  
Date: [today]  
Clinician: [licensed MHP]

Symptoms endorsed (mild–moderate intensity):
- Loss of enjoyment / anhedonia (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)
- Marked generalized & nocturnal anxiety, panic episodes (Q4, Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed / difficulty coping (Q6)
- Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worries (Q7)
- Intermittent sadness, “heavy” mood, late-afternoon dips (Q8)
- Episodic tearfulness, though no sustained crying spells (Q9)

Denies:
- Suicidal ideation or self-harm thoughts (Q10)

Pattern: Symptoms cluster around anxious-arousal, low mood, and maternal self-doubt; functionally impairing rest and daily management. No current safety concerns.

Screening significance: Score suggests elevated distress consistent with possible postpartum depression ± anxiety; warrants follow-up with formal assessment (e.g., PHQ-9, GAD-7) and discussion of supports/interventions.
